title: Passive I — direct passive られる

grammarPoints.rule: Two shapes, one job. An u-verb (godan) rides the same stem grid you already know from ば and volitional, but lands on the A-ROW: shift the dictionary form's final -u sound back to its -a partner, add れる — ぬすむ → ぬすま + れる = ぬすまれる, かう → かわ + れる = かわれる. An ichidan (ru) verb does what it always does — drop る, add the ending whole: ほめる → ほめ + られる = ほめられる. The two irregulars are two words to memorize outright: する → される, くる → こられる. Notice ichidan られる and godan れる are close cousins — both are 'the verb, plus something-reru' — but only ichidan gets the extra ら.

examples.ja: ぬすむ → ぬすまれる
ほめる → ほめられる

antiPattern.why: られる only glues straight onto a verb that already ends in a vowel stem (ichidan) — an u-verb has to bend to its a-row FIRST: ぬすむ → ぬすま, then + れる. ぬすまれる.

grammarPoints.rule: Turn the sentence around: the person something happens TO becomes the topic, marked は/が, and the person who DOES it takes に — the passive's agent marker. がくせいは せんせいに ほめられた: the student is the one it happened to; the teacher is who did it. This is not always bad news, despite what 'passive voice' might suggest — せんせいに ほめられた IS good news (I was praised), がくせいは せんせいに しかられた is bad news (was scolded) — the GRAMMAR carries no judgment either way; the verb's own meaning does all of that work. One quirk to file away: for an ichidan verb, られる is the exact same shape as the potential form (たべられる can mean 'is eaten' OR 'can eat') — context is what tells them apart, the same way English 'can' does double duty.

examples.ja: がくせいは せんせいに しかられた。
examples.en: The student was scolded by the teacher.

examples.ja: せんせいに ほめられた。
examples.en: I was praised by the teacher.

examples.ja: せんせいに しつもんされた。
examples.en: I was asked a question by the teacher.

antiPattern.ja: がくせいは せんせいを しかられた。
antiPattern.why: the AGENT of a passive — the one doing it — takes に, not を: を would mark it as a direct object, as if the student did the scolding. せんせいに しかられた。

grammarPoints.rule: When what got affected is something you OWN, Japanese keeps that thing marked を and makes the OWNER the topic instead — the opposite of English, which promotes the owned thing to subject ('my wallet was stolen'). どろぼうに さいふを ぬすまれた literally sits as '[I], by-a-thief, wallet, was-stolen' — わたしは is usually dropped because it's obvious, but さいふ keeps を the whole time. It never becomes さいふは ぬすまれた unless you're talking about the wallet itself, not about what happened to you.

examples.ja: どろぼうに さいふを ぬすまれた。
examples.en: My wallet was stolen (by a thief).

examples.ja: どろぼうに とけいを ぬすまれた。
examples.en: My watch was stolen (by a thief).

antiPattern.ja: さいふが どろぼうを ぬすまれた。
antiPattern.why: the owned thing keeps を; it's the OWNER who becomes the topic, not the wallet: (わたしは) どろぼうに さいふを ぬすまれた。

grammarPoints.rule: For who MADE something — an invention, a building, a discovery — the agent often takes によって instead of plain に, especially in written or explanatory Japanese: この きかいは タナカさんに よって はつめいされた, this machine was invented by Mr. Tanaka. によって sits exactly where に would, marking the agent — it's a more formal cousin, reserved for creation and authorship. Plain に still works and is what you'll hear in conversation; agentless is common too, when the maker doesn't matter: この きかいは けんきゅうされた, this machine was researched (by nobody named).

examples.ja: この きかいは タナカさんに よって はつめいされた。
examples.en: This machine was invented by Mr. Tanaka.

examples.ja: この いえは ちちに よって たてられた。
examples.en: This house was built by my father.

examples.ja: この きかいは けんきゅうされた。

antiPattern.ja: タナカさんは この きかいを はつめいされた。
antiPattern.why: the CREATED THING is the topic of a creation-passive, not its maker — swap them: この きかいは タナカさんに よって はつめいされた。

grammarPoints.rule: Some Japanese passives have no English passive to match at all. あめに ふられた doesn't mean 'was rained' — it means something happened TO you and it was a nuisance: I got rained on. ふる (to fall, rain/snow) never takes an object in its plain form — nothing 'does' the raining to anyone — yet the passive still exists, purely to mark that the speaker was inconvenienced by it. どろぼうに はいられた works the same way: a burglar broke in (on me), and I'm the one who suffered for it. Recognize this shape for now — production comes later; for today, just hear the flavour it carries that plain sentences don't.

examples.en: I got rained on (and it was a pain).

examples.ja: どろぼうに はいられた。
examples.en: I had a burglar break in on me.

antiPattern.why: this passive isn't about the rain — it's about the person it happened to, marked with に, same as every other passive agent: あめに ふられた。

beats.en: I was called in by the police.

lessons.title: Challenge — the day the police came
lessons.focus: Every passive pattern in one arc — mechanical formation, direct に, possessed-object を, creation によって — combined with prior N4 grammar, no new vocabulary

beats.ja: どろぼうに さいふを ぬすまれたので、けいさつに でんわした。
beats.en: Since my wallet was stolen by a thief, I called the police.

beats.ja: どろぼうは けいさつに そうさされたし、きずも あった。
beats.en: The thief was investigated by the police, and what's more he had a wound.

beats.stem: この きかいは タナカさん
beats.answer: によって
beats.en: This machine was invented by Mr. Tanaka.
beats.explanation: によって is に + よって — the more formal cousin, reserved for who MADE something.
